newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai official denies Cambodia's Pol Pot in exile.
newsitem.headline: Thai official denies Cambodia's Pol Pot in exile.

text.p: A Thai general with long involvement in policy toward Cambodia on Friday dismissed reports that Cambodia's notorious rebel leader Pol Pot had gone into exile in Thailand or China.

The general said talk in the Cambodian capital that Khmer Rouge guerrilla leader Pol Pot and two of his top commanders had gone into exile appeared to be a result of a long-running feud between Cambodia's two prime ministers, Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen.
"Thailand will never accept Pol Pot for political exile or allow him to travel via our soil to another country," the general, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
"The reports are a result of the political conflict between Ranariddh and Hun Sen. They're trying to drag Thailand and China into it again," he said.
Pol Pot was still in the rebels' northern Cambodia stronghold at Anlong Veng according to the latest information, he said.
"No country wants to get involved with the Khmer Rouge any more, everyone knows that getting into this will only have negative consequences," he said.

General Nhiek Bun Chhay, a Cambodian general loyal to Ranariddh, told the Cambodia Daily newspaper this week that Pol Pot and two other top guerrilla commanders had agreed to abandon their jungle strongholds and go into exile while allowing their troops to defect to the government.

Khieu Samphan, the nominal head of the guerrilla group whose reputation is seen as less tarnished than that of Pol Pot and his two right-hand men, would be allowed to enter politics, the paper quoted Nhiek Bun Chhay as saying.
The Cambodian government has not confirmed the report although military officials said negotiations with the Khmer Rouge were under way.

The Khmer Rouge, responsible for the death of more than one million people during their 1975-1979 "killing fields" rule, has been hard hit by government offensives, defections and splits since boycotting a 1993 election.

But although they have been seriously weakened, the guerrillas have again become a political factor as a result of the feud between Cambodia's two premiers who are both striving to bolster their strength in the run-up to an election due next year.

Political analysts in Phnom Penh said Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party was trying to woo Khieu Samphan into a political alliance. But to gain politically from such an agreement, Ranariddh would have to be able to assure the Cambodian people that the hated Pol Pot was not part of the deal, the analysts said.
Hun Sen was eager to head off any such agreement as it could be a threat to his political position, the analysts said.
Hun Sen warned in a speech on Thursday that Khieu Samphan would not be allowed to return to Phnom Penh and he would be physically attacked by the people if he came back.
Thailand and China supported a three-party guerrilla alliance, which included the Khmer Rouge and royalist forces, during the Cambodian war in the 1980s.
All outside powers agreed to cease assisting all Cambodian factions under a 1991 peace treaty signed in Paris.
